analysis.title: Stronger October jobs data, still gradual hikes
key_insights: October nonfarm payrolls rose 165k versus consensus of 70k. Strength was broad, led by private services excluding leisure and hospitality.

August and September payrolls were revised up by a combined 84k. The three-month average payroll gain is now about 137k, up from the 51k pace previously reported, and above estimates of the job growth needed to keep unemployment stable.
The low rate of implied layoffs in claims data may explain the stronger report.

The unemployment rate edged down 3bps to 4.14% (rounds to 4.1%). It has stayed in a 4.1-4.3% range since March. Participation rose a tenth to 61.9% and the employment-to-population ratio rose to 59.3%, which points to a labor market near full employment.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.4% m/m and 3.1% y/y versus consensus of 0.3% and 2.9%. Annual wage growth is still on a softening trend, so the y/y rate declined despite the stronger monthly gain.
Aggregate private payroll income growth strengthened to 4.4% y/y on a three-month moving-average basis, which supports consumption.

Weakness was concentrated in leisure and hospitality (employment down 13k) and housing-related sectors (residential construction and home-related retail down about 32k combined). Housing industries remain exposed to higher interest rates.
UBS expects 25bps Fed hikes in December and March, slightly more tightening than markets price, with about 1.9 additional hikes priced cumulatively through 3Q27.

With 4Q growth tracking around 2%, the labor data make it hard to argue policy is clearly restrictive. Stable unemployment and wage growth near 3% limit the case for a more aggressive tightening campaign than a recalibration hiking cycle.
